Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Breaking Bad Tokens: Detoxification of LLMs Using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used to detoxify large language models by steering activations in the residual stream, and what are the trade-offs between toxicity reduction and model fluency?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for detoxifying LLMs, introducing a three-tiered steering approach that offers trade-offs between toxicity reduction and language fluency.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based causal interventions are promising for LLM detoxification but have limitations such as fluency degradation and feature splitting, suggesting practical guidelines for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering significantly reduces toxicity, outperforming existing baselines at higher steering strengths.
Strong steering can degrade fluency in some models (e.g., GPT-2 Small) but not in others (e.g., Gemma-2-2B).
Model capabilities on standard NLP benchmarks remain stable after steering.
Feature splitting in wider SAEs hampers detoxification performance, but a composition-based approach can mitigate this.
The method is interpretable and does not require additional data at inference time.
papers.limitation:
The method may not generalize to all forms of toxicity, especially subtle or context-dependent harms.
Manual SAE feature selection is labor-intensive and may overlook some toxic features.
Results are shown on specific layers; other layers may yield different results.
Fluency degradation in GPT-2 Small is a limitation.
future_direction: Developing scalable and robust approaches for feature identification.
Exploring layer-wise effects more comprehensively.
Extending to other safety concerns beyond toxicity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now ubiquitous in user-facing applications, yet they still generate undesirable toxic outputs, including profanity, vulgarity, and derogatory remarks. Although numerous detoxification methods exist, most apply broad, surface-level fixes and can therefore easily be circumvented by jailbreak attacks. In this paper we leverage sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify toxicity-related directions in the residual stream of models and perform targeted activation steering using the corresponding decoder vectors. We introduce three tiers of steering aggressiveness and evaluate them on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2-2B, revealing trade-offs between toxicity reduction and language fluency. At stronger steering strengths, these causal interventions surpass competitive baselines in reducing toxicity by up to 20%, though fluency can degrade noticeably on GPT-2 Small depending on the aggressiveness. Crucially, standard NLP benchmark scores upon steering remain stable, indicating that the model's knowledge and general abilities are preserved. We further show that feature-splitting in wider SAEs hampers safety interventions, underscoring the importance of disentangled feature learning. Our findings highlight both the promise and the current limitations of SAE-based causal interventions for LLM detoxification, further suggesting practical guidelines for safer language-model deployment.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Evaluating and Designing Sparse Autoencoders by Approximating Quasi-Orthogonality
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be evaluated and designed with a theoretical grounding for sparsity, avoiding the need to manually tune the hyperparameter k?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Approximate Feature Activation (AFA), a theoretical framework linking input embedding norms to sparse feature activation norms, and top-AFA, an activation function that adaptively selects the number of active features per input without tuning k.
papers.conclusion: The AFA framework addresses a core limitation in SAE design by providing a principled way to link input embeddings to feature activations, and top-AFA SAE demonstrates improved performance over fixed-sparsity methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed top-AFA SAE outperforms top-k and batch top-k SAEs in reconstruction performance on GPT-2 layers.
The εLBO metric provides a different evaluation perspective on SAE quality compared to mean squared error (MSE).
The AFA formulation provides a closed-form estimate of the ℓ2-norm of sparse activations with provable error bounds.
Pre-trained SAE decoders often fail to achieve the level of quasi-orthogonality permitted by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
Top-AFA allows adaptive per-input sparsity, removing the need for a fixed sparsity hyperparameter k.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis is limited to the linear representation hypothesis; extending AFA to more general superposition settings remains an open question.
Top-AFA introduces a new hyperparameter λAFA and can result in high ℓ0 values.
future_direction: Extending AFA to more general superposition settings, such as when Φ(·) is a two-layer neural network or other SAE variants like Matryoshka SAEs.
A deeper investigation into the necessity of the loss coefficient λAFA.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used in mechanistic interpretability research for large language models; however, the state-of-the-art method of using $k$-sparse autoencoders lacks a theoretical grounding for selecting the hyperparameter $k$ that represents the number of nonzero activations, often denoted by $\ell_0$. In this paper, we reveal a theoretical link that the $\ell_2$-norm of the sparse feature vector can be approximated with the $\ell_2$-norm of the dense vector with a closed-form error, which allows sparse autoencoders to be trained without the need to manually determine $\ell_0$. Specifically, we validate two applications of our theoretical findings. First, we introduce a new methodology that can assess the feature activations of pre-trained SAEs by computing the theoretically expected value from the input embedding, which has been overlooked by existing SAE evaluation methods and loss functions. Second, we introduce a novel activation function, top-AFA, which builds upon our formulation of approximate feature activation (AFA). This function enables top-$k$ style activation without requiring a constant hyperparameter $k$ to be tuned, dynamically determining the number of activated features for each input. By training SAEs on three intermediate layers to reconstruct GPT2 hidden embeddings for over 80 million tokens from the OpenWebText dataset, we demonstrate the empirical merits of this approach and compare it with current state-of-the-art $k$-sparse autoencoders. Our code is available at: https://github.com/SewoongLee/top-afa-sae.

papers.title: Feature Extraction and Steering for Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs without external datasets by extracting features from vanilla Chain-of-Thought and steering internal states?
papers.core_contribution: A framework that extracts reasoning features from vanilla CoT via verbal/symbolic decomposition and steers LLM activations to enhance reasoning without external datasets or retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature extraction and steering methods enhance reasoning in LLMs, and the SAE-free approach extends the benefits to models without corresponding SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering improves accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SAE-free steering works without pre-trained SAEs and achieves comparable or better performance.
Steering increases reasoning length and attention to mathematical tokens.
There is an optimal steering strength; too high strength degrades performance.
The method suppresses noisy features and amplifies task-relevant reasoning features.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning datasets.
Experiments are limited to three model families (LLaMA, DeepSeek, Gemma).
future_direction: Extend to more diverse reasoning domains such as logical reasoning, scientific problem-solving, or multi-step planning.
Apply the method to more diverse LLM architectures to verify generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to solve reasoning and mathematical problems using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique. Expanding CoT length, as seen in models such as DeepSeek-R1, significantly enhances this reasoning for complex problems, but requires costly and high-quality long CoT data and fine-tuning. This work, inspired by the deep thinking paradigm of DeepSeek-R1, utilizes a steering technique to enhance the reasoning ability of an LLM without external datasets. Our method first employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from vanilla CoT. These features are then used to steer the LLM's internal states during generation. Recognizing that many LLMs do not have corresponding pre-trained SAEs, we further introduce a novel SAE-free steering algorithm, which directly computes steering directions from the residual activations of an LLM, obviating the need for an explicit SAE. Experimental results demonstrate that both our SAE-based and subsequent SAE-free steering algorithms significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Route Sparse Autoencoder to Interpret Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively extract interpretable features from multiple layers of a large language model, overcoming the limitations of single-layer sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a framework that integrates a lightweight routing mechanism with a shared sparse autoencoder to dynamically and efficiently extract interpretable features from multiple layers of a language model's residual stream.
papers.conclusion: RouteSAE is a powerful tool for understanding and intervening in the internal representations of LLMs, providing a scalable and effective method for feature discovery and interpretability-driven model interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Under the same sparsity constraint, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more interpretable features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score.
RouteSAE achieves a lower KL divergence at the same sparsity level compared to baseline SAEs, indicating better reconstruction quality and feature relevance for language modeling.
RouteSAE successfully captures both low-level features (e.g., word-level polysemy) from shallow layers and high-level features (e.g., sentence-level patterns) from deep layers within a unified feature space.
The routing mechanism assigns weights in a U-shaped distribution across layers, balancing the use of shallow and deep layers rather than concentrating on a subset.
RouteSAE enables targeted feature steering by manipulating feature activations, allowing controlled intervention on the model's output behavior.
papers.limitation:
The router employs a simple linear projection, which has limited capabilities; its weight distribution is influenced by the feature space size and sparsity level.
The current method of dynamically selecting activations across layers is not yet optimized for discovering cross-layer features.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated activation aggregation methods and router designs.
Enabling RouteSAE to more effectively identify and utilize cross-layer features.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models (LLMs) aims to uncover the internal processes of information propagation and reasoning. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated promise in this domain by extracting interpretable and monosemantic features. However, prior works primarily focus on feature extraction from a single layer, failing to effectively capture activations that span multiple layers. In this paper, we introduce Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a new framework that integrates a routing mechanism with a shared SAE to efficiently extract features from multiple layers. It dynamically assigns weights to activations from different layers, incurring minimal parameter overhead while achieving high interpretability and flexibility for targeted feature manipulation. We evaluate RouteSAE through extensive experiments on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Specifically, under the same sparsity constraint of 64, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score. These results underscore the potential of RouteSAE as a scalable and effective method for LLM interpretability, with applications in feature discovery and model intervention. Our codes are available at https://github.com/swei2001/RouteSAEs.

papers.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a given sparsity level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JumpReLU SAEs, a simple modification of ReLU SAEs that achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level and is similarly interpretable to other SAE methods.
papers.conclusion: JumpReLU SAEs are a mild improvement over prevailing SAE training methodologies, offering better or equal reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity, similar interpretability, and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
JumpReLU SAEs consistently provide more faithful reconstructions than Gated SAEs and at least as good as, and often slightly better than, TopK SAEs at a given sparsity level.
JumpReLU SAEs have few dead features without the need for resampling during training.
JumpReLU SAEs have a similar proportion of very high frequency features (active on >10% of tokens) as TopK SAEs, which is higher than Gated SAEs.
Manual and automated interpretability studies show that JumpReLU SAE features are similarly interpretable to Gated and TopK SAE features.
JumpReLU SAEs are efficient to train, requiring no auxiliary loss terms and having an elementwise activation function (unlike TopK).
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are conducted on a single model (Gemma 2 9B), raising uncertainty about transfer to other models.
The science of principled evaluations of SAE performance is still in its infancy; it is unclear how well current metrics correlate with downstream utility.
JumpReLU SAEs tend to have relatively more very high frequency features than Gated SAEs.
JumpReLU SAEs introduce new hyperparameters (initial threshold and bandwidth) that require selection.
future_direction: Evaluate SAEs on a broader selection of metrics that more directly correspond to the value SAEs add by aiding or enabling downstream tasks, such as circuit analysis or model control.
Further tweak the loss function used to train JumpReLU SAEs to directly tackle the phenomenon of high frequency features.
Develop more principled ways to choose hyperparameters, such as the bandwidth parameter, possibly borrowing from kernel density estimation literature.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising unsupervised approach for identifying causally relevant and interpretable linear features in a language model's (LM) activations. To be useful for downstream tasks, SAEs need to decompose LM activations faithfully; yet to be interpretable the decomposition must be sparse -- two objectives that are in tension. In this paper, we introduce JumpReLU SAEs, which achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level on Gemma 2 9B activations, compared to other recent advances such as Gated and TopK SAEs. We also show that this improvement does not come at the cost of interpretability through manual and automated interpretability studies. JumpReLU SAEs are a simple modification of vanilla (ReLU) SAEs -- where we replace the ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU activation function -- and are similarly efficient to train and run. By utilising straight-through-estimators (STEs) in a principled manner, we show how it is possible to train JumpReLU SAEs effectively despite the discontinuous JumpReLU function introduced in the SAE's forward pass. Similarly, we use STEs to directly train L0 to be sparse, instead of training on proxies such as L1, avoiding problems like shrinkage.

papers.title: Evaluating Open-Source Sparse Autoencoders on Disentangling Factual Knowledge in GPT-2 Small
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature spaces are useful for causal interpretability analysis, specifically for disentangling related factual knowledge (country and continent of cities) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Current open-source sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for GPT-2 small struggle to provide a feature space that better disentangles factual knowledge than the baseline of neurons, and none approach the performance of the supervised DAS skyline.
papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Encode Scientific Quality? An Empirical Study Using Monosemantic Features from Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concept of scientific quality using monosemantic features extracted from sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic investigation into how LLMs encode scientific quality using monosemantic features from sparse autoencoders, identifying four key types of features related to research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode a rich and multidimensional representation of scientific quality through monosemantic features, capturing aspects like research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon, providing insights into their internal mechanisms for research evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode features reflecting research methodologies, associating higher quality with rigorous methodological approaches.
Features related to publication type, such as survey papers and literature reviews, are associated with higher scholarly impact.
Features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies act as strong signals of perceived research importance.
Features corresponding to specific scientific jargons and academic language are identified, though their precise role is unclear.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of monosemantic features inherently involves a qualitative component, as semantic labels are assigned by human researchers and may introduce subjectivity.
This work focused exclusively on Gemma 2 models, limiting the generality of the results to other architectures.
The study classified publications into research quality quartiles rather than using regression to predict specific values.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other LLM architectures to assess the generality of the results.
Using regression to predict specific quality values instead of classification into quartiles.
Investigating how interpretable features can enhance LLM performance in tasks such as research evaluation, academic text generation, and hypothesis discovery.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing use of generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) in particular, to support both the assessment and generation of scientific work. Although some studies have shown that LLMs can, to a certain extent, evaluate research according to perceived quality, our understanding of the internal mechanisms that enable this capability remains limited. This paper presents the first study that investigates how LLMs encode the concept of scientific quality through relevant monosemantic features extracted using sparse autoencoders. We derive such features under different experimental settings and assess their ability to serve as predictors across three tasks related to research quality: predicting citation count, journal SJR, and journal h-index. The results indicate that LLMs encode features associated with multiple dimensions of scientific quality. In particular, we identify four recurring types of features that capture key aspects of how research quality is represented: 1) features reflecting research methodologies; 2) features related to publication type, with literature reviews typically exhibiting higher impact; 3) features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies; and 4) features corresponding to specific scientific jargons. These findings represent an important step toward understanding how LLMs encapsulate concepts related to research quality.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: AudioSAE: Towards Understanding of Audio-Processing Models with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively applied to audio-processing models to obtain stable, interpretable features, and do these features have practical utility?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces AudioSAE, applying sparse autoencoders to audio models (Whisper and HuBERT), demonstrating that they yield stable, interpretable features capturing acoustic and semantic information, and shows practical utility in hallucination reduction and correlation with human EEG.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are effective tools for interpreting audio-processing models, providing stable and interpretable features that have practical applications such as hallucination reduction and show alignment with human neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
Over 50% of SAE features remain consistent across random seeds.
SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events like environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds.
Features disentangle concepts effectively, requiring removal of only 19–27% of features to erase a concept.
Feature steering reduces Whisper’s false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase.
SAE features are correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing.
papers.limitation: The auto-interpretation method depends on empirically selected thresholds and is biased by the predominance of speech data in the test set, potentially obscuring rarer music or sound events, and is limited by the capabilities of the underlying audio captioning model.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are powerful tools for interpreting neural representations, yet their use in audio remains underexplored. We train SAEs across all encoder layers of Whisper and HuBERT, provide an extensive evaluation of their stability, interpretability, and show their practical utility. Over 50% of the features remain consistent across random seeds, and reconstruction quality is preserved. SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events, including environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds (e.g. laughter, whispering) and disentangle them effectively, requiring removal of only 19-27% of features to erase a concept. Feature steering reduces Whisper's false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase, demonstrating real-world applicability. Finally, we find SAE features correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing. The code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/audiosae/audiosae_demo.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Sparse Modular Activation for Efficient Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn to activate their attention modules on demand to achieve better quality-efficiency trade-off? How much extra attention is needed for the SSMs on a task-by-task basis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism for sparsely and dynamically activating sub-modules in neural networks, and applies it to design SeqBoat, a novel hybrid SSM-GAU architecture that achieves significantly better quality-efficiency trade-offs in sequence modeling.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Modular Activation (SMA) enables efficient and interpretable dynamic module activation, and its application in SeqBoat demonstrates superior quality-efficiency trade-offs across diverse sequence modeling tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SeqBoat achieves new state-of-the-art average accuracy among linear-complexity hybrid models on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark.
SeqBoat provides substantial training speedup and memory reduction compared to Transformer and other baselines, e.g., 10.4x speedup and 95% memory reduction on the LRA Text task.
The learned sparse activation patterns of the GAU module directly reveal the amount of attention needed for each task and data sample.
The working memory mechanism in SeqBoat enables linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span and outperforms chunking-based models.
SeqBoat achieves competitive performance on speech classification (Speech Commands) and language modeling (enwik8) with improved efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation of SMA is I/O bounded due to copying large tensors with scatter operations, and no custom fused kernels were used for memory bandwidth optimization.
Experiments were limited to models of moderate size due to computational resource constraints, leaving scalability to larger models uncertain.
future_direction: Explore the scaling behavior of SMA and how to incorporate it with pre-trained large language models.
Investigate the interpretability of module activation patterns and their correlation with input tokens or model predictions.
Scale up SMA with a large number of modules, potentially impacting Mixture-of-Experts research.
papers.abstract: Recent hybrid models combining Linear State Space Models (SSMs) with self-attention mechanisms have demonstrated impressive results across a range of sequence modeling tasks. However, current approaches apply attention modules statically and uniformly to all elements in the input sequences, leading to sub-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism enabling neural networks to sparsely and dynamically activate sub-modules for sequence elements in a differentiable manner. Through allowing each element to skip non-activated sub-modules, SMA reduces computation and memory consumption of neural networks at both training and inference stages. To validate the effectiveness of SMA on sequence modeling, we design a novel neural architecture, SeqBoat, which employs SMA to sparsely activate a Gated Attention Unit (GAU) based on the state representations learned from an SSM. By constraining the GAU to only conduct local attention on the activated inputs, SeqBoat can achieve linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span, and provide substantially better quality-efficiency trade-off than the chunking-based models. With experiments on a wide range of tasks, including long sequence modeling, speech classification and language modeling, SeqBoat brings new state-of-the-art results among hybrid models with linear complexity, and reveals the amount of attention needed for each task through the learned sparse activation patterns. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/renll/SeqBoat.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of concept representations in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to adversarial input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces robustness as a critical evaluation dimension for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and demonstrates that SAE concept representations are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations.
papers.conclusion: SAE interpretations are highly vulnerable to minimal input changes, raising concerns about their reliability in realistic settings, and motivating the development of more robust interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate SAE concept representations without notably affecting the base LLM's activations.
SAE concept representations are not robust even to non-adversarial synonym replacements.
The attacks are effective across different models, datasets, and model depths.
Untargeted attacks are more successful at the population level, while targeted attacks are more effective at the individual level.
SAE latents that represent meaningful concepts are highly manipulable.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of attacks is bounded by compute constraints (single 80GB A100 GPU).
The choice of medium-sized LLMs results in slower attacks.
future_direction: Developing novel methods to denoise SAE activations and isolate reliable signals.
Extending the evaluation framework to other concept-extraction tools like transcoders and crosscoders.
Optimizing the attack pipeline to better balance effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly used to interpret the internal activations of large language models (LLMs) by mapping them to human-interpretable concept representations. While existing evaluations of SAEs focus on metrics such as the reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff, human (auto-)interpretability, and feature disentanglement, they overlook a critical aspect: the robustness of concept representations to input perturbations. We argue that robustness must be a fundamental consideration for concept representations, reflecting the fidelity of concept labeling. To this end, we formulate robustness quantification as input-space optimization problems and develop a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring realistic scenarios in which adversarial perturbations are crafted to manipulate SAE representations. Empirically, we find that tiny adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate concept-based interpretations in most scenarios without notably affecting the base LLM's activations. Overall, our results suggest that SAE concept representations are fragile and without further denoising or postprocessing they might be ill-suited for applications in model monitoring and oversight.

papers.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a duality framework between SAE architectures and concept geometry, showing that SAEs impose implicit assumptions about concept structure, and proposes a new SAE (SpaDE) that explicitly incorporates nonlinear separability and concept heterogeneity to recover previously hidden concepts.
papers.conclusion: There is no universal SAE architecture; the choice of SAE should be guided by the geometry of concepts in the model's representations, and data-aware design is essential for effective interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are not universal; their architecture imposes implicit assumptions about concept structure (e.g., linear separability, uniform dimensionality) that bias what they can detect.
Existing SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK) fail to recover concepts that are nonlinearly separable or have heterogeneous intrinsic dimensionality.
The proposed SpaDE SAE, which uses a sparsemax projection and Euclidean distances, can adaptively capture concepts with nonlinear separability and heterogeneous dimensionality.
Experiments on synthetic data, formal languages, and vision activations validate that SpaDE discovers concepts missed by other SAEs and maintains clearer concept boundaries.
The duality between SAE architecture and concept geometry suggests that interpretability tools must be designed with the data's concept structure in mind.
papers.limitation:
SpaDE assumes that Euclidean distances are meaningful in the concept space, which may not hold for all datasets.
The duality framework currently covers ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, and SpaDE, but may not generalize to all SAE variants.
Experiments are limited to synthetic data, a formal language, and one vision dataset (Imagenette); broader validation is needed.
future_direction: Extend the duality framework to other SAE architectures and interpretability methods.
Automate the selection of SAE architecture based on data properties.
Explore more complex concept structures beyond nonlinear separability and heterogeneity.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret neural networks by identifying meaningful concepts from their representations. However, do SAEs truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts? We introduce a unified framework that recasts SAEs as solutions to a bilevel optimization problem, revealing a fundamental challenge: each SAE imposes structural assumptions about how concepts are encoded in model representations, which in turn shapes what it can and cannot detect. This means different SAEs are not interchangeable -- switching architectures can expose entirely new concepts or obscure existing ones. To systematically probe this effect, we evaluate SAEs across a spectrum of settings: from controlled toy models that isolate key variables, to semi-synthetic experiments on real model activations and finally to large-scale, naturalistic datasets. Across this progression, we examine two fundamental properties that real-world concepts often exhibit: heterogeneity in intrinsic dimensionality (some concepts are inherently low-dimensional, others are not) and nonlinear separability. We show that SAEs fail to recover concepts when these properties are ignored, and we design a new SAE that explicitly incorporates both, enabling the discovery of previously hidden concepts and reinforcing our theoretical insights. Our findings challenge the idea of a universal SAE and underscores the need for architecture-specific choices in model interpretability. Overall, we argue an SAE does not just reveal concepts -- it determines what can be seen at all.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: SplInterp: Improving our Understanding and Training of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the theoretical understanding and training of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) using spline theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies spline theory to understand SAEs, showing they are piecewise affine splines that generalize k-means autoencoders, and introduces the PAM-SGD training algorithm which improves sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.conclusion: The spline theory lens provides insight into SAEs, and PAM-SGD is a promising training method with advantages in sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are piecewise affine splines, and TopK SAEs correspond to Kth-order power diagrams.
SAEs generalize k-means autoencoders but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability compared to the optimal piecewise affine autoencoder (which combines k-means with local PCA).
The proposed PAM-SGD algorithm for training SAEs has solid theoretical foundations and shows promising empirical results, especially in low-data regimes and improved sparsity.
papers.limitation:
The spline geometry characterization is currently limited to TopK SAEs.
The bridge between SAEs and PCA-based autoencoders sets aside the matter of shared decoding vectors.
PAM-SGD makes approximations that break assumptions of the theory and had some empirical limitations (e.g., instability with TopK in LLM experiments).
future_direction: Extending the spline geometry characterization beyond TopK SAEs.
Exploring the incorporation of geometry into SAE training.
